intro: After the loud drinking song, a solo oboe, muted strings and one alto voice: frost on the grass, a cold wind, a lamp that has gone out, a heart that is tired. This is the second song of one live 1939 Amsterdam performance of the whole cycle, with a chamber-like orchestra that has no trumpets, trombones or percussion.
question: How does a weary orchestra hold a listener through ten slow minutes?

sections.label: A · D minor — autumn mist and frost
B · The scent gone, the cold wind
A′ · Tempo I — the weary heart
sections.mNote: opening tempo and shuffling strings return under new words

sections.label: D · Mit großem Aufschwung — sun of love
Coda · Tempo I subito — the postlude

cues.title: Oboe over shuffling violins
cues.text: Muted first violins shuffle in unbroken eighth notes while a solo oboe sings, marked molto espress. The heading is Etwas schleichend. Ermüdet — somewhat creeping, weary. No trumpet, trombone or percussion is scored anywhere in this song; the orchestra is closer to chamber music.
cues.evidence: The first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; IMSLP #20582, printed p. 39) gives the heading, the oboe solo and the muted violins; the Mahler Foundation orchestration page lists wind solos for this song. The recording rises from −32 dB at 0:00 to about −14 dB by 0:25, with D minor estimated at 0:20–0:35 (correlation 0.79–0.84).

cues.title: A weaver’s poem becomes autumn
cues.text: The source is a poem by the Tang court poet Qian Qi, “Imitating the Old Poem: Long Autumn Night”, about a woman weaving by a failing lamp. Judith Gautier’s French turned its first half into a lonely speaker’s autumn evening; the weaving woman was left out.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Der Einsame im Herbst page (http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Einsame.htm) prints Qian Qi’s poem beside Gautier’s “Le soir d’automne”, marking the half Gautier did not translate; Wikipedia, Long Autumn Night, reports Qian Renkang’s identification in 1983 and its confirmation in 1999; Edwin K. C. Li, JRMA 150/2 (2025), fn 3.

cues.title: A flute echo, then the voice
cues.text: A flute marked Echo answers the oboe, and soon the alto enters in D minor with “Herbstnebel wallen bläulich überm See” — autumn mists drift blue over the lake.
cues.evidence: The score (printed p. 40) marks Echo in the flute and the alto’s entry with Etwas zurückhaltend, and says the alto part may be sung by a baritone; local key estimates read D minor with correlation 0.74–0.83 at 1:10–1:20. The alto’s entry time is not claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fließend: the frost spreads
cues.text: Around 1:35 the level jumps by about nine decibels and the report detects roughly twice as many attacks. The marking is Fließend (flowing) and the violins take their mutes off; a horn sings a long line marked “edel gesungen” — nobly sung — while the alto describes the frost covering every blade of grass.
cues.evidence: Level rises from −19.6 dB at 1:30 to −10.2 dB at 1:35 and onset density from 2.8 to 5.4 and 6.2 per second at 1:35–1:40 (roughly double); a boundary at 1:52 (0.73) follows. The score (printed p. 40) has Fließend, Dämpfer ab! and a horn marked p molto espr. (edel gesungen).

cues.title: A low chord under “Blüten”
cues.text: Around 2:10 the alto reaches the first stanza’s last line, “über die feinen Blüten ausgestreut” — scattered over the fine blossoms. Stopped horns, bassoons and bass clarinet underline it with a low sforzando-piano chord, one of the five loudest windows of the song.
cues.evidence: The level climbs from −22.9 dB at 2:05 to −7.1 dB at 2:15, which is one of the five loudest windows in the report, with a boundary at 2:10 (0.80) and very low brightness (about 890–920 Hz). The score (printed p. 41) has stopped horns, bassoons and bass clarinet marked sfp at the start of that line.

cues.title: The first song of the cycle
cues.text: The Mahler Foundation’s chronology puts this song’s composition in July 1908, the first of the six, at Toblach. The same month Mahler told Bruno Walter he could not work at a desk: “for my inner activity I need outer activity”, and his doctors had restricted his long walks.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, History: Das Lied von der Erde (https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-history/): composition of Lied 2 in July 1908; Stephen E. Hefling for Universal Edition quotes the letter of 18 July 1908 and the doctors’ restrictions: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: “Ein kalter Wind”
cues.text: In the second stanza the sweet scent of the flowers is gone, and a cold wind bends their stems. The alto’s line is marked schauernd — shuddering — and clarinets trill beneath; onsets reach five or six a second in several windows between 3:15 and 3:35.
cues.evidence: Onset density is 6.0, 5.0 and 5.4 per second at 3:15, 3:20 and 3:25 and 6.0 at 3:35, with a boundary at 2:46 (0.64); the score (printed p. 42) has schauernd over the alto’s line, clarinet trills and pp sehr gehalten for the preceding line about the vanished scent.

cues.title: Golden leaves on the water
cues.text: Tempo I subito, marked zögernd (hesitating): “Bald werden die verwelkten, goldnen Blätter der Lotosblüten auf dem Wasser ziehn” — soon the faded golden lotus petals will drift on the water. The alto sings it “with tender expression”, and a solo cello answers.
cues.evidence: The score (printed p. 43) has the text, Tempo I subito (zögernd), the alto’s mit zärtlichem Ausdruck and a cello marked Solo. The loud window at 3:55 (−6.9 dB, one of the five loudest) lies just before the interlude; individual entrances are not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Zart drängend: the voice stops
cues.text: Around 4:06 the singer leaves and the orchestra alone plays Zart drängend — tenderly pressing on. The violins are marked zart leidenschaftlich, tenderly passionate, over winds and horns, and a long rise begins that takes close to half a minute.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 4:06 (0.71) with the level falling to −22.3 dB at 4:15 and then rising to −6.6 dB at 4:35. The score (printed p. 43, rehearsal figure 10) has Zart drängend and zart leidenschaftlich for the violins, with no vocal part until figure 11.

cues.title: The peak and the collapse
cues.text: Around 4:35 the orchestra reaches its fullest point: a sustained, loud chord with almost no new attacks. Then the level falls by more than twenty decibels within twenty seconds, and the cellos, marked wieder zurückhaltend, sink to pppp. Listen for the stillness after it.
cues.evidence: Level is −6.6 dB at 4:35 with 0.8 onsets per second, then −12.4, −21.6, −26.1 and −29.5 dB at 4:40, 4:45, 4:50 and 4:55; the strongest boundary of the song is 4:40 (1.00). The score (printed p. 44) has ff and Wieder zurückhaltend, with the cellos marked dim. to pppp.

cues.title: Tempo I: “Mein Herz ist müde”
cues.text: Tempo I. Nicht eilen — do not hurry. The opening speed and shuffling strings return, now under “Mein Herz ist müde. Meine kleine Lampe erlosch mit Knistern”: my heart is weary; my little lamp went out with a crackle. Mutes are back on the strings, and the tone is ohne Ausdruck, without expression.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 4:58 (0.85) and onset density rising to 6.8 per second at 5:00 after the near-silence of 4:50–4:55. The score (printed p. 44, rehearsal figure 11) has Tempo I, Nicht eilen, mit Dämpfer, ohne Ausdruck and the text.

cues.title: A heart that tires
cues.text: A year before he chose these words, a doctor at Maiernigg found a valvular defect in Mahler’s own heart, later confirmed by a Vienna specialist. It was not in itself fatal, but it left him open to the endocarditis that killed him in 1911.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s introduction for Universal Edition: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538 (diagnosis in July 1907 after Maria’s death, the Vienna specialist, the link to bacterial endocarditis, death four years later). The poem’s line is Bethge’s; no causal claim is made.

cues.title: A plea for rest
cues.text: Around 6:00 the harmony brightens towards a major key for “Ich komm zu dir, traute Ruhestätte! Ja, gib mir Ruh” — I come to you, dear resting place; give me rest. The alto’s line is marked innig, heartfelt, and the pace is Nicht schleppen: do not drag.
cues.evidence: The local key estimate reads D major at 6:00–6:10 (correlation 0.73, 0.60 and 0.44 by 6:15) after a loud 5:55 window (−8.4 dB), then the level falls to −27 dB by 6:25. The score (printed p. 45) has Nicht schleppen, innig and the text; the estimate is not a chord identification.

cues.title: “Ich weine viel”
cues.text: Back in D minor around 6:55 for “Ich weine viel in meinen Einsamkeiten” — I weep much in my solitudes. A flute marked molto espress. leads over running violin figures, and the key estimate at 7:00–7:05 shows a strong D minor.
cues.evidence: D minor is estimated with correlation 0.85 and 0.88 at 7:00 and 7:05, level near −7 dB at 7:00. The score (printed p. 46, rehearsal figure 16) has the text, a flute marked molto espress. and continuous violin sixteenth notes.

cues.title: “Sonne der Liebe”
cues.text: From about 7:30 the strings and winds swell for “Der Herbst in meinem Herzen währt zu lange”, two harps sweep in unison arpeggios, and at Mit großem Aufschwung — with great upsurge — the alto sings “Sonne der Liebe, willst du nie mehr scheinen?” Sun of love, will you never shine again? The key estimate reads E♭ major.
cues.evidence: Onset density reaches 6.0–7.2 per second at 7:30–7:35, E♭ major is estimated at 7:40–7:55 (0.75–0.78) and 7:55 is among the five loudest windows (−7.2 dB); boundaries at 7:42 and 7:46. The score (printed pp. 47–48) has Fließend, ff harp arpeggios and Mit großem Aufschwung with three flats.

cues.title: Tempo I subito: the question
cues.text: Around 8:05 the level drops by about twelve decibels. After a Drängend swell and a held ff, Tempo I subito returns and the alto asks, “mild aufzutrocknen?” — to dry my bitter tears gently. Mahler’s “mild” is his own addition to Bethge’s line.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −11.0 dB at 8:00 to −23.6 dB at 8:05 with the strongest late boundary at 8:08 (0.91). The score (printed p. 49, rehearsal figure 19) marks Drängend then Tempo I subito over a sparse texture; the Mahler Archives page shows Bethge’s line without “mild”.

cues.title: Premiere and the baritone option
cues.text: Bruno Walter conducted the first performance, in Munich on 20 November 1911, six months after Mahler’s death, with Sara Cahier and William Miller. The score allows a baritone for this song; Walter tried a baritone once and decided tenor and alto worked better.
cues.evidence: IMSLP work page (https://imslp.org/wiki/Das_Lied_von_der_Erde,_GMW_49_(Mahler,_Gustav)) for the Munich Tonhalle premiere; the score (printed p. 40) for the baritone note; Mahler Foundation, History page, for Walter’s trial with Friedrich Weidemann.

cues.title: The oboe leaves last
cues.text: In the postlude the oboe, bassoon and horn sing fragments over the violins, and the opening shuffle fades. The score closes on a Rit. with pp and morendo, dying away. By about 9:10 the level is about 30 dB below the song’s loudest moment; the last half-minute is very quiet.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −19.6 dB at 8:45 to −31 to −33 dB at 9:10–9:25 and −36.1 dB at 9:35. The score (printed p. 50) has Rit., pp, morendo and ppp for the final bars.

transitions.title: A loud chord falls to a hush
transitions.how: The first stanza ends on the low sforzando-piano chord of stopped horns, bassoons and bass clarinet beneath “Blüten”, and the level falls away. The second stanza begins pp sehr gehalten (very restrained) for “Der süße Duft der Blumen ist verflogen”, then shivers as the cold wind arrives. The tune, shuffling strings and slow pace stay; the sound is thinner and quieter.
transitions.evidence: Level is −7.1 dB at 2:15 and −15.4 and −22.7 dB at 2:55 and 3:00, with a boundary at 2:46 (0.64). The chord and markings are read from printed pp. 41–42 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: The voice leaves; the strings press on
transitions.how: After the alto’s “auf dem Wasser ziehn” the voice is silent for nearly a minute. The marking Zart drängend (tenderly pressing on) sets violins and violas to a tender, passionate line over winds and horns, with the solo cello leading then joining tutti. The harmony and register rise in a long ascent, so the tempo does not so much change as lean forward.
transitions.evidence: A boundary at 4:06 (0.71); level falls to −22.3 dB at 4:15 and rises to −6.6 dB at 4:35. Markings, solo cello and tutti are read from printed p. 43 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Collapse, then Tempo I
transitions.how: The interlude’s ff climax, marked Wieder zurückhaltend (again holding back), is followed by a diminuendo to pppp in the cellos. Then Tempo I. Nicht eilen returns the opening pace and shuffling strings, with mutes, and the alto begins “Mein Herz ist müde”. The return comes by exhaustion: the first tempo is what is left once the swell has gone.
transitions.evidence: Strongest boundary 4:40 (1.00) and 4:58 (0.85); level −6.6 dB at 4:35, −29.5 dB at 4:55, onset density 6.8 per second at 5:00. Markings are read from printed p. 44 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Harps and a rising swell
transitions.how: Over “Der Herbst in meinem Herzen währt zu lange” the strings and winds swell to ff, and two harps sweep upward in unison arpeggios. At Mit großem Aufschwung (“with great upsurge”) the key signature has three flats, E♭ major, and the alto leaps to “Sonne der Liebe”. The harps, absent from every earlier page of this song, carry the swell to its crest.
transitions.evidence: Onset density 6.0–7.2 per second at 7:30–7:35, E♭ major estimated at 7:40–7:55 and the loudest-window ranking at 7:55 (−7.2 dB), with boundaries at 7:42 and 7:46. Markings and harp parts are read from printed pp. 47–48 of the 1912 full score.

transitions.title: Drängend, then a question in a hush
transitions.how: Harp arpeggios and a pressing Drängend carry the climax over “um meine bittern Tränen”, then Tempo I subito arrives at once. The alto sings the last words, “mild aufzutrocknen?”, p ohne Ausdruck, over pizzicato cellos. A question mark ends the text; the orchestra answers with a long postlude, mostly oboe, bassoon and violins.
transitions.evidence: Level falls from −11.0 dB at 8:00 to −23.6 dB at 8:05 and the late boundary 8:08 (0.91) follows. Drängend, Tempo I subito, p ohne Ausdruck and the text are read from printed pp. 49–50 of the 1912 full score.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, II. Der Einsame im Herbst, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: IMSLP #20582; printed pp. 39–50. Entry times are proportioned between audio anchors at 1:35, 2:10, 4:06, 4:40, 4:58, 7:40 and 8:08 and are approximate; which edition the 1939 orchestra used is not documented.

timeline.note: A solo oboe sings over muted first violins in shuffling eighth notes.
Clarinets and horns join; both violin sections shuffle.
Violas and cellos add their voices; the flute echoes the oboe.
The alto enters over a flute echo, soft winds and strings.
Fließend: a horn sings a long line while the alto describes the frost.
Stopped horns, bassoons and bass clarinet underline “Blüten” with a low chord.
Second stanza: very restrained, with thin woodwinds and violas.
The cold wind: a prominent oboe and trembling strings under the alto.
A solo cello answers the alto’s tender lines about the golden leaves.
Zart drängend: the voice is silent and the strings climb with winds and horns.
The peak: sustained ff winds, horns and strings before the collapse.
Tempo I: the muted shuffle returns under “Mein Herz ist müde”.
The plea “Ich komm zu dir, traute Ruhestätte”, with muted horns and strings.
A flute leads over running violins as the alto weeps in solitude.
Two harps sweep in unison as the whole orchestra swells to the sun of love.
Tempo I subito: the alto’s last question over pizzicato cellos.
The postlude: oboe, bassoon and horn above the violins’ shuffle.
A last oboe and clarinet line fades over the first violins.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: No catalogue number is given for the source of this file.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No acetate matrix, side or take numbers appear in the sources consulted; this is not a claim that they cannot be recovered.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item names an uploader account but no transfer or restoration engineer; an uploader is not automatically a transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Internet Archive derivatives of a WAV original: this file is a variable-bit-rate MP3 (169 kbps); FLAC and spectrogram derivatives of the same WAV are also listed.
fields.note: The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
